claims.text: The starting material is crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals.
Introducing a controlled amount of oxide dispersion can enhance the operational stability of the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
The oxide dispersion pins grain boundaries in the nanoparticles.
Grain-boundary pinning by the oxide dispersion prevents excessive grain growth.
Preventing excessive grain growth enhances nanoparticle stability.
Oxide-dispersion-treated nanoparticles will be more stable than untreated nanoparticles.
Oxide-dispersion-treated nanoparticles will have improved catalytic performance relative to untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed intervention is applicable while retaining a near-equiatomic solid-solution alloy containing five or more metals.
The relevant temperature boundary for the intervention is 773–1173 K.
Some refractory high-entropy alloys are plausible candidates for elevated-temperature applications.
The optimal oxide amount, oxide type, and synthesis method have not yet been determined.
X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can be used to compare structural stability of treated and untreated nanoparticles after high-temperature operation.
Catalytic activity measurements can be used to compare catalytic performance of treated and untreated nanoparticles.
